snippet.title: Advice for time traveling to medieval Europe
snippet.description:
Watch this video before visiting the European Middle Ages.

SUGGESTED READING

• Steven A. Epstein, An Economic and Social History of Later Medieval Europe, 1000–1500 (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2009).
• Urban Tignor Holmes, Jr., Daily Living in the Twelfth Century (Madison: University of Wisconsin Press, 1952).
• Ian Mortimer, The Time Traveller's Guide to Medieval England (London: The Bodley Head, 2008).
• Paul B. Newman, Daily Life in the Middle Ages (Jefferson, N.C.: McFarland & Company, 2001).
• Jeffrey L. Singman, Daily Life in Medieval Europe (Westport, Conn.: Greenwood Press, 1999).


FAQ

• What about traveling there as a woman?
My advice applies to both men and women (except for the bit about clergy, obviously). Men and women will have to give the same amount of attention to constructing their backstory, including their marital status, because people will ask either way. Women went on pilgrimages. While most women (and men) worked on farms, women in towns did engage in economic activities like shopkeeping and weaving. It was rare for a woman to work as a long-distance merchant, but it did happen, typically as a widow whose husband had been a merchant.

• But what about a woman traveling alone?
When I said, "Travel in a group, don't travel alone," I meant it. Solo travel is not advised, regardless of gender. Even the medieval people themselves traveled in groups.


CORRECTIONS

• I said William of Rubruck was from the Netherlands but he was actually Flemish. Apologies to my Flemish viewers.
• In the anecdote where William of Rubruck met the Buddhist monks, he was confused at first but he did figure out in the course of talking to them that they were not Christian. I misremembered the passage. So I'd say Buddhists would probably just be understood as pagans in medieval Europe.
• The magic I discuss in the video is known as natural magic. There was also another form of magic I didn't talk about where you perform occult rituals to persuade demons to do things for you. That's known as demonic magic.

snippet.title: Why You Wouldn't Survive Medieval Food for Even 3 Days!
snippet.description:
buymeacoffee.com/History.Unleashed

Ready for more time travel? ⏳ A little caffeine boost powers my next jump into the past! Thanks for being part of the journey. ☕️

You dream of a sumptuous medieval banquet with roasted wild boar and golden wine? Forget it. If you were transported back to the year 1250 today, a knight's sword wouldn't be your biggest threat—your dinner would be. Your modern, sterile body wouldn't survive this culinary war for more than three days.

snippet.description:
What was it really like to survive a medieval winter as a peasant under serfdom? We break down the Great Famine of 1315, when wheat prices in England soared 700% and millions starved. You'll learn how families survived in longhouses alongside livestock, breathing toxic wood smoke from open hearths, and how ergotism — known as Saint Anthony's Fire — turned contaminated rye bread into a hallucinogenic poison. We cover the Great Bovine Pestilence, the Black Death that killed up to 60% of Europe's population, and how centuries of suffering finally erupted into the Peasants' Revolt led by Wat Tyler. This is the Middle Ages they don't teach you in school.

Sources and Further Reading

Bartholomaeus Anglicus (c. 1240). On the Properties of Things (Medieval encyclopedia, on seasons and natural phenomena).

Langland, William (1378). Piers Plowman (Middle English allegorical poem depicting peasant life and hardships).

Anonymous (1393). Le Ménagier de Paris (The Goodman of Paris) – Medieval household guide (on managing food and winter provisions).

Laumonier, Lucie (2020). “A Medieval Peasants’ Winter” (Medievalists.net article on winter climate and peasant life).

Navea-Rogers, Tizane (2025). “Surviving the Medieval Midwinter” (Historic UK, on clothing, food, and winter activities in medieval Britain).

Singman, Jeffrey L. (1999). Daily Life in Medieval Europe (overview of everyday routines, including seasonal patterns).

Jones, Richard (2013). The Medieval Natural World (study of medieval climate and environmental conditions).

Gies, Frances & Gies, Joseph (1990). Life in a Medieval Village (detailed social history of peasants, with sections on winter living).

Benedict of Nursia (6th cent., rule codified c. 540). The Rule of St. Benedict (monastic rulebook, Chapter 55 on clothing allowances in cold climates).

Jordan, William Chester (1996). The Great Famine: Northern Europe in the Early Fourteenth Century (historical analysis of famine and climate impact around 1315–17).

How did people survive a medieval winter without modern heating or technology? This video explores the harsh realities of life in the Middle Ages—how peasants, nobles, and monks prepared for the cold, stored food, kept warm, and fought off illness and famine. Learn about medieval clothing, shelter, diet, and survival strategies that kept communities alive through months of darkness and snow. Perfect for history enthusiasts and anyone fascinated by everyday life in the past.

snippet.title: How Medieval Peasants Survived Winter Without Freezing – Genius Cold Hacks from the Middle Ages!
snippet.description:
Think medieval peasants just froze all winter? Think again. ❄️🔥
In this deep dive into life during the coldest months of the Middle Ages, we explore how ordinary people survived brutal winters without modern heating, insulation, or even decent windows.

🏠 Underground homes? Check.
💩 Poop-insulated walls? Yep.
🔥 A central hearth that did it all? Absolutely.

From clever house designs dug into the earth, to wattle-and-daub walls (yes, with real manure), to the warm heart of every home—the central hearth—we uncover the surprisingly smart and resourceful ways peasants kept cozy when temperatures plummeted.

🔍 Based on recent archaeological discoveries and historical reconstructions, this video uncovers the real story of winter survival in medieval times. It’s not just history—it’s a medieval masterclass in DIY insulation.

👉 Watch to find out how your ancestors stayed warm when the only thing colder than the weather was the draft blowing through their tiny windows.

🛖 Like, comment, and subscribe for more epic tales of survival, smarts, and medieval life!

snippet.title: Why You Would Not Survive 24H in Medieval London
snippet.description:
We imagine Medieval London as a city of knights, chivalry, and romance. In reality, it was a biological death trap. If you traveled back to 1350 today, your modern immune system would likely collapse within 24 hours.

This documentary by "History Unleashed" takes you on a sensory tour of a city paved not with gold, but with excrement. Discover why the River Thames was both the main sewer and the drinking fountain, and why locals drank weak ale from dawn till dusk just to stay alive.

We analyze the daily horrors: From "Saint Anthony's Fire" (hallucinations caused by fungal bread) to the "Gong Farmers" who shoveled human waste from cesspits by hand. Learn why the murder rate was 50 times higher than today and why a simple walk down Cheapside was a game of Russian Roulette involving falling chamber pot contents and cutthroats.

From heads displayed on pikes to surgery without anesthesia—this is the true, dystopian story of the city that never slept, because it was too dangerous to close your eyes.

Have you ever been curious about Medieval life? Would you travel back in time if you could? Do you think you would enjoy it? How long would you last? Hear ye, hear ye! The Middle Ages sucked!
